8. Turning to the genesis behind the contract the witness stated that the title deeds of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were not with him. He, however, consulted the title deed Exhibit C. The vendors were introduced to him on the same day. The vendors had equal shares as per their document of title. The witness further stated that the entries in the S. A. Khatian Exhibit 2 were not without foundation. He, however, feels shy to explain the sources for payment of Tk. 37,000/- on the day of contract Defendant No. 1 was a non-Bengalese and in February, 1971 defendant Nos. 1 and 2 left for Karachi where he met them to demand execution and registration of the kabala. He, however, disclosed his ignorance whether or not there were Bhatia’s in the disputed promises in 1970. According to this witness defendant No. 1 came back to Dacca from Karachi in February, 1971. He admitted that defendant No. 1 on repatriation came back to Dacca in 1974. He also admitted that two storied building on the suit premises was a new one. The witness denied the interpolation in different places in that Baina patra Exhibit 1 including the erasing figure “4". He also denied that the Hand Writing Expert was gained over for favorable report. 

 15. Mr. Abdus Salam, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal has taken us through the pleadings, evidence and the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge. Mr. Salam contends that the learned Subordinate Judge should have held that defendant No. 1 executed the agreement Exhibit 1 on 16.11.70. According to the learned Advocate, the evidence on record proves the fact of execution of the Bainapatra by the defendant No. 1.We have gone through the evidence and Mr. Salam has also taken us through the oral evidence of P.W.s. P.W. 2 is a man under direct influence of plaintiff No. 1. P.W. 3 is a man who cannot be relied upon on the ground that he appeared to be omnibus on matters of plaintiffs' interest. He is a vegetable dealer and in course of his normal profession he was not supposed to be acquainted with the plaintiffs or defendant No. 1. He is not an attesting witness of Exhibit 1. He has admitted that he is unlettered. Therefore, there was no occasion to bring such an unlettered man to witness the execution of an agreement involving a heavy amount of money. He was worthless for the purpose of attestation. To our minds it appears that that he is unreliable for the purpose of proving the contract as he did nothing in respect of the transaction which he sought to prove as a Mokabila witness. P.W.4 speaks nothing about the contract. Thus apart from the oral evidence of P.W.1 there is no re-liable evidence to prove the fact' of execution of the Baina patra Exhibit 1 by defendant No. 1 on receipt of Tk. 37,000/- on 16.11.70. It is surprising to notice the umbra behind the genesis of the contract. There is no disclosure that the plaintiffs had acquaintance with defendant No. 1 There is no-thing on record to indicate that 'Dalai' or middleman approached the parties in negotiating the deal. How plaintiffs and defendant No. 1 came in contact and how the negotiation took place have been left undisclosed by the plaintiffs. The plaintiff did not introduce the story of agreement with a necessary pre-face or introduction. The less said about D.W. 2 is best for all. There is nothing on record to indicate except Ext. 2 S.A. Khatian, that defendant No. 2 is any way connected with the disputed property. In view of document of title Exhibit C there is no scope to hold that defendant No. 2 was still holding an interest in the disputed premises. It will not be too wild to think that taking hold of S A khatian the whole story was cooked up and the agreement Exhibit 1 was brought into being in the names of defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The plaintiffs are silent as regards the title of defendant No. 2. 

 18. Mr. M. H. Khondker, the learned Advocate for the respondent No: 1 has contended that the Expert's opinion is a piece of evidence and it is neither conclusive nor binding so far as the court is concerned. According to him the court is the Expert and law provides the court with jurisdiction to examine the disputed signatures. Mr. Khondkar has referred to section 73 of the Evidence Act and also has relied upon some decisions to which we shall presently refer, in support of his contention. But on a consideration of the contentions of the learned Advocates, it may be stated at-the outset that Mr. Salam stands on a sandy soil. There is hardly any foundation behind his contention which he seeks to support by relying upon a decision in the case of Md. Nurul Huq Mia and another v. The State (1). In a criminal appeal, the question arose as to what extent reliance can be given on comparison made by the court under section 73 of the Evidence Act in support of a conviction. In that context it was held that it would be unsafe to base a conviction upon the result of comparison by the court. It does not appear that this decision laid down a proposition in generality. On the other hand, in the case of Manindra Chandra Lala v. The Mahaluxmi Bank Limited, (2) their Lordships of the Privy Council held that the court was competent to examine the signature under section 73 of the Evidence Act and that the learned Judges themselves looked into the apparent similarity of the signatures appearing in the it bugged Will of that case. It, therefore, justifies that the court power of examination under section 73 of the Evidence Act is not restricted by the decision referred to aid relied upol by Mr. Salam. Mr, Khondker has also referred to another decision in the case of Sreemati Sarojini Dassi v. Hari Day Ghose (3) This was also a case arising out of a probate proceeding and comparison of the handwriting by the court was "deemed a made of ascertaining the truth which ought to be used with very great caution". In the case of Bisseswar Poddar v. Nabadwip Chandra Poddar and another (4) a similar view was expressed relying upon the two decisions we have referred to above. In respectful agreement with the views expressed in the afore-said decisions we hold that the Court's power to examine signatures under section 73 of the Evidence Act is not restricted but the court has to exercise the power with great caution. It may be mentioned that arbitrary exercise of the power may lead to miscarriage of justice. In an appropriate case watered the court finds that the exercise of its power is necessary in the interest of justice the court may exercise its enabling power under section 73 of the Evidence Act. In the instant case the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have exercised his powers under section 73 of the Evidence Act and it is evident that the learned Subordinate Judge did so with great caution, We have ourselves looked into the signatures of Salma Khatun. It is a pointer to note that Salma Khatun never described herself as 'Salema Khatun' although she signed her name in Urdu. In all her signature except these appearing in the Baina patra she has consistently spelt her name as Salma Khatun. The only exception appears in Exhibit where she was described as Salema Khatun. It appears to be beyond human conduct to mutilate one's name consistently. The evidence is that defendant No. 1 a lady of letters, knows Bengali as well as Urdu. In all her writings, we find that it is legible and clear. In all the specimen signatures she described herself correctly as Salma Khatun. She was never under any constraint while she executed Exhibit C, the deed of lease. If we compare her signatures appearing in Exhibit C with those appearing in Exhibit 1 the apparent dissimilarity is patent even to the naked eyes. She was pointedly asked the question by confronting her with the signatures appearing in Exhibit 1; she stoutly denied the signatures as her own. Therefore, it is idle to think that the signatures appearing in Exhibit 1 were under the same hand of the signatory in Exhibit C. All other specimen signatures of her name as Salma Khatun tallied with her signatures though out. The signatures appearing in Exhibit 1 appear to be only exception. This exception, in our opinion, has been manufactured by the plaintiffs with a definite motive behind. In the khatian Exhibit 2, we find her name has been spelt as Salema Khatun. The clue was taken from there and it was applied in the manufacturing; of Exhibit 1. There is nothing on record to indicate that the plaintiffs were in possession of any signagures of Salma Khatun prior to Exhibit 1. knowing her to be a Non-Bengalee, her signatures in Urdu were manufactured in Exhibit 1 in the light of the spelling appearing in Exhibit 2. It may not be too far to think that Exhibit 2 also provided the basis of the association of the name of Abdul Syed Khan with that of defendants No. 1. It further suggests that the names of the defendants were taken from Exhibit 2 and were incorporated in Exhibit 1 as spelt in Exhibit 2. There is no evidence as against Ext. C to indicate any nexus in the interest between defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Defendant No. 2 is a fictitious man.
